summary: The fourth MIME document. It specifies registration procedures for MIME facilities with IANA, such as media types. It is a best current practice, and it was replaced by RFC 4288 and RFC 4289.

eli5.summary: It explains how to put a new kind of email content on the official list.

subtitle: The rules for adding new media types, access types and transfer encodings to MIME through IANA.

tldr.problem: MIME is open-ended, so new media types, external-body access types and transfer encodings keep arriving. Without a registration process the set of values would not be orderly, well specified or public.
tldr.mechanism: IANA acts as the central registry. Media types are registered in trees (IETF, vendor, personal) with different requirements, access types go through a reviewer, and new transfer encodings must be standards-track RFCs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2048 is a Best Current Practice that obsoleted RFCs 1521, 1522 and 1590. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 4288 and RFC 4289 and updated by RFC 3023.

today: RFC 2048 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 13) that has been obsoleted by RFC 4288 and RFC 4289, and updated by RFC 3023. It obsoleted RFC 1521, RFC 1522 and RFC 1590.

sections.title: Why MIME Needs Registration
sections.content:
RFC 2048 is the fourth of the MIME documents. MIME, the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, redefines message formats to allow non-ASCII text, an extensible set of non-textual body formats, multi-part bodies and non-ASCII header text. MIME is an open-ended framework that can take on new object types, character sets and access methods without changing the basic protocol, but a registration process is needed so these values are developed in an orderly, well-specified and public manner.

This document defines procedures that use the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as the central registry. It covers three things: media types, external body access types and content-transfer-encodings. Registration of character sets is covered elsewhere and is no longer addressed here.

The RFC includes a historical note. The media type process was first defined for asynchronous Internet mail, where limiting the number of types helped interoperability when the remote system's capabilities were unknown. As media types are used in new environments, that original procedure was excessively restrictive and had to be generalized.
sections.eli5: Many people keep inventing new kinds of files and ways to send them. The rule is that every new kind must be written down in one public list so everyone knows what it is called and how it works.

sections.title: Registration Trees for Media Types
sections.content:
Media type names can be faceted (tree.subtree...type), and the leading facet identifies the registration tree. Each tree has different requirements and a different owner.

  • The IETF tree is for types of general interest. It requires IESG approval and publication as some form of RFC. Names are normally not faceted, and the IETF owns the registration.
  • The vendor tree uses the leading facet vnd. for types tied to commercially available products. Anyone who needs to interchange files for the product may register, but the registration belongs to the vendor. It may be submitted directly to IANA.
  • The personal or vanity tree uses prs. for experimental types or those from products not distributed commercially. The registrant owns it, and it may be submitted directly to IANA.
  • The special x. tree is for unregistered, experimental types, like names starting with x-. Its use, and use of the x- form, is discouraged because the simplified vendor and personal procedures make it rarely necessary.

IANA may, with the advice and consent of the IESG, create additional top-level trees, for example for well-known permanent bodies such as scientific societies.
sections.eli5: There are different shelves. One is for official, community-approved types, one for companies' own file types, one for personal projects, and one for experiments that you should try to avoid using.

sections.title: What a Media Type Registration Must Satisfy
sections.content:
Every registration must meet a set of requirements, some of which vary by tree. A media type must function as an actual media format. Things better thought of as a transfer encoding, a character set or a collection of separate entities cannot be registered, so base64 cannot be registered as a media type. Every type needs a type and subtype name; the top-level type must fit the nature of the media, and a new top-level type can only be defined by a standards-track RFC.

Parameters must be fully specified for the IETF tree and should be as complete as possible for the vendor and personal trees. All registered types must use a single canonical data format. A precise, openly available format specification is required for the IETF tree, while the vendor tree may only name the software and version that produce or process the type. The personal tree still needs a format specification, which may be deposited with IANA and need not be public. Patented technology is permitted, but the limits in RFC 1602 must be respected for standards-track protocols.

A security analysis is required for IETF tree types and encouraged for others. Whatever is said must be accurate: a statement that there are no security issues must not be confused with the issues not having been assessed. Universal implementation is not a registration requirement, and a type intended for limited use should say so.
sections.eli5: Before a new file type gets on the list it must really be a kind of file, have a clear name, and be described well enough that others can use it. If it has any safety risks, its owners must say so honestly.

sections.title: The Registration and Change Procedure
sections.content:
The procedure is an administrative one run by IANA, not a formal standards process. For the IETF tree, the normal IETF process applies, with an Internet-Draft and an announcement on the ietf-types list as a first step. For the vendor and personal trees, the review step may be skipped and the template sent directly to IANA, though community review is encouraged.

In the review step, the proposed registration is sent to ietf-types@iana.org for a two week review period. Proposed types are not formally registered and must not be used; the x- prefix can be used until registration is complete. IETF tree types must then be approved by the IESG, and IANA registers the type. IANA registers vendor and personal types automatically provided minimal conditions are met: the type is a real media format, names are properly formed with the correct tree prefix, personal types give or point to a format specification, and any security considerations are not obviously bogus.

For changes, the owner follows the same path: publish the revised template, leave at least two weeks for comments, and publish through IANA after formal review if required. Registrations may not be deleted; a type no longer believed appropriate can be marked OBSOLETE in its intended use field. The IESG may reassign responsibility, for example when the author has died or cannot be reached. Anyone may send comments on a registered type to IANA, which passes them to the owner.
sections.eli5: You show your idea to a mailing list for two weeks so people can comment. For official types a committee has to approve it. For company or personal types you can send it straight in. Once on the list a type is never erased, only labeled as old.

sections.title: Access Types and Transfer Encodings
sections.content:
The message/external-body media type lets an entity point at the real body data instead of containing it. Each reference names an access type that says how to retrieve it. A new access type needs a unique name, a fully public description of every protocol and procedure it uses (secret or proprietary methods are prohibited), a complete description of known security issues, and an RFC, which may be informational. The proposal goes to ietf-types for two weeks. An access type reviewer, appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director, then forwards it to IANA or rejects it because of significant objections. The reviewer's decision must be posted within 14 days and can be appealed to the IESG.

Transfer encodings transform a media type after it is in canonical form, for example base64 and quoted-printable to survive text-only transports, or compression. The RFC says that standardizing many transfer encodings is a barrier to interoperability and is expressly discouraged. A new one must have a unique name, a fully described algorithm, work on any sequence of octets, document its output range (7bit, 8bit or binary), be fully invertible (which excludes lossy compression and encryption), and provide some new functionality. It must be defined by a standards-track RFC with substantial justification, and the IESG notifies IANA when one is approved.
sections.eli5: Two other lists work the same way. One lists the different ways to fetch a file that is stored somewhere else. The other lists ways to repackage data so it travels safely. The rules strongly say: do not invent new packaging unless you really have to.
